topics.description: A Dutch chartered trading company founded in 1602 that conducted commerce and colonial activity across Asia and the Indian Ocean.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This empire’s Periwig Era saw its strong currency deter trade, coining the name for an economic “disease.” The term rangaku referred to books sold by this empire’s traders on the island of Dejima near Nagasaki. This empire’s navy relied on the fluyt and included ships called Sea Beggars. This empire was home to the (*) VOC, the most valuable company of all time. The first stock markets emerged in this empire whose economy experienced a bubble from tulip trading. Land reclamation projects begun in this empire created polders and were drained by now-iconic windmills. For 10 points, name this empire that was centered in Holland.
parts.answer: ANSWER: Dutch Empire [or the Netherlands; or the Dutch Republic; or the United Provinces of the Netherlands; or the United Provinces; or the Republic of the Seven United Netherlands; or the Kingdom of the Netherlands; or Nederlands; accept the Dutch East India Company; accept Dutch Learning; accept Dutch disease; prompt on Holland before mention]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The decline of this country’s industrial sector in the mid-18th century is derisively known as the “Periwig Era.” This country’s colonial ventures were overseen by companies operated by the 19 Gentlemen and 17 Gentlemen. This country’s financial innovations included hosting the first publicly traded company and the first (*) stock exchange. This country expanded its farmland and created a vast system of polders using windmills. In the 1630s, a speculative bubble drove up the price of tulips in this country, then collapsed dramatically. For 10 points, name this European country whose stock exchange was hosted in Amsterdam.
parts.answer: The Netherlands [or Kingdom of the Netherlands or Nederland or Koninkrijk Nederlanden accept Dutch Republic or Republic of the Seven United Netherlands or United Provinces of the Netherlands]

topics.description: A southeastern European country comprising a mainland and numerous islands in the Aegean and Ionian seas, with Athens as its capital.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Much of the information about this group’s attempted conquest of Egypt was derived from inscriptions and reliefs at Medinet Habu. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this confederation of people, whose origin remains mysterious. This group contributed to the fall of empires like the Mycenaeans and Hittites during the Bronze Age Collapse.
parts.answer: Sea Peoples

parts.label: B
parts.question: The Sea Peoples may have allied with a group called “Ahiyyawa” from this country. According to Homer, a confederation from this modern-day country fought Troy in the Trojan War.
parts.answer: Greece [or the Hellenic Republic; or Ellas; or Elliniki Dhimokratia]

parts.label: C
parts.question: Unlike most Mediterranean polities, some Phoenician cities peaked after the Bronze Age collapse, such as this Tunisian city founded by Dido. This city’s army was once run by the Barca family.
parts.answer: Carthage [or Kart-hadasht; or Colonia Julia Carthago; or Karchedon]

topics.topic: Charge of the Light Brigade (1854 military action)
topics.description: A disastrous British cavalry charge during the Battle of Balaclava in the Crimean War on 25 October 1854.
aliases: Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava
Charge of the Light Brigade (military action)

parts.label: L
parts.question: During this war, Florence Nightingale gained the nickname “The Lady With the Lamp” for nursing  injured soldiers. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [10] Name this war fought over a peninsula in the Black Sea between Russia and an Ottoman-European  alliance.
parts.answer: Crimean War

parts.label: B
parts.question: [10] This failed 1854 military action against Russian forces occurred during the Battle of Balaclava and  was the subject of a poem about 600 soldiers marching “into the valley of Death.”
parts.answer: the Charge of the Light Brigade

parts.label: C
parts.question: [10] The Charge of the Light Brigade was led by this British lord and Major-General, whose name now  refers to a garment that he is credited with inventing during the war.
parts.answer: Lord Cardigan [or James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan]

topics.description: A medieval and early modern commercial and defensive alliance of northern European cities and merchant guilds centered on trade around the North and Baltic Seas.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Valdemar Atterdag plundered the city of Visby during his war with this organization. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this trade confederation that operated trading posts called kontors in cities like Lübeck. This trade confederation was active in Northern Europe, especially the Baltic.
parts.answer: Hanseatic League [or Hansa]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Valdemar Atterdag was the king of this country that was eventually forced to sign the Treaty of Stralsund with the Hanseatic League. Valdemar was the first king of this country to rule from its current capital of Copenhagen.
parts.answer: Kingdom of Denmark

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] Valdemar earlier sold the province of Danish Estonia to this other organization. This organization had previously lost the 1242 Battle of the Ice to the forces of Novgorod under Alexander Nevsky.
parts.answer: Teutonic Knights [or the Teutonic Order or Order of Brothers of the German House of Saint Mary in Jerusalem; prompt on the Livonian Order with “what larger organization was it part of?”]

parts.label: L
parts.question: In 1907, this region's parliament, the Løgting (LEK-ting), instituted a ban on alcohol that remained in  effect until 1992. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [10] Name this archipelago, which was occupied by the British in Operation Valentine starting with its  capital Tórshavn (TEH-oosh-AO-win).
parts.answer: Faroe Islands [or the Faroes; or Føroyar; or Færøerne]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [10] After the Napoleonic Wars, the Faroe Islands became part of this mainland country, whose World  War II-era king Christian X (the tenth) was also the only King of Iceland.
parts.answer: Denmark [Kingdom of Denmark; or Kongeriget Danmark]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [10] Danish control of the Faroe Islands began after the Kingdom of Norway entered the Kalmar Union,  which opposed this medieval coalition of merchant guilds around the North and Baltic seas.
parts.answer: Hanseatic League [or Hansa]

topics.description: A horse-drawn, spoked-wheeled vehicle used in ancient warfare, transport, ceremonies, and racing.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This son of Akhenaten ruled with the assistance of the vizier Ay ("eye"), who eventually succeeded him after his death. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [10] Name this "Boy Pharaoh" of Egypt, whose tomb was famously discovered nearly intact by Howard Carter.
parts.answer: Tutankhamun [or Tutankhaten, or King Tut, or Twt- nḫ-jmn, or Tawat ʕanḥu Aman]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [10] During his reign, Tutankhamun moved Egypt's capital from Amarna back to this other city. This city shares its name with a city-state in Greece that was legendarily founded by Cadmus.
parts.answer: Thebes [or Thēbai; accept Waset, even though this name technically only applies to the Thebes in Egypt and not the Thebes in Greece]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [10] According to one theory, Tutankhamun's premature death may have been caused by an accident involving one of these vehicles. In ancient Rome, spectators could watch these vehicles at the Circus Maximus.
parts.answer: chariots [accept quadriga]

topics.description: The fortified barrier constructed in 1961 that divided East and West Berlin until its opening and subsequent dismantling in 1989.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This structure was destroyed after Gunther Schabowski’s accidental declaration that a policy would go into effect “immediately.” Peter Fechter [fesh-ter] bled to death at this structure as guards threatened to (*) shoot potential helpers. “Brain drain” was meant to be prevented by this “anti-fascist bulwark.” Checkpoint Charlie was a border control on, for ten points, what structure that, until 1989, separated East and West Germany within a capital city?
parts.answer: Berlin Wall

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Lucius Clay organized Operation Vittles to deliver supplies to a portion of this city. Checkpoint Charlie was the best-known location for crossing a structure in this city. A two-year Soviet blockade of this city was countered by its namesake (*) “Airlift.” Ronald Regan asked Mikhail Gorbachev to “tear down” a structure in this city. For 10 points, a wall separated the capitalist West from the communist East portion of what German capital?
parts.answer: Berlin [accept Berlin Airlift or Berlin Wall] <European History–Kapadia>

topics.description: The historic city on the Bosporus that served as the capital of the Eastern Roman and Byzantine Empires and is now known as Istanbul.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: In this modern-day country, the seventh of an ancient city’s nine layers shows scorch marks consistent with a foreign siege. The neolithic cities of Catalhoyuk and Gobekli Tepe are located in this country, where Heinrich Schliemann excavated the site of ancient (*) Troy. This country was home to the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire. For 10 points, name this modern-day country once called “Asia Minor,” where the Hittites complained about people from Constantinople.
parts.answer: Turkey [or the Republic of Turkey; or Turkiye Cumhuriyeti]

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this city where during that defense a besieging fleet was supposedly hauled over land into the Golden Horn. The army protecting this city retreated to the Blachernae palace after the Theodosian walls were overrun.
parts.answer: Constantinople [or Konstantiniyye]

parts.label: B
parts.question: Constantinople fell in 1453 to this empire. This empire ruled much of the Balkans and the Middle East until it was dissolved and became the modern Republic of Turkey.
parts.answer: Ottoman Empire

parts.label: C
parts.question: The mercenaries led by Giustiniani primarily hailed from this city. Andrea Doria served as a capable admiral for and governed this Italian city-state, which was a maritime rival of Venice in the Mediterranean Sea.
parts.answer: Genoa [or Genova]

topics.description: South Africa is the sovereign country at the southern tip of Africa, associated in these clues with its geography, apartheid-era history, literature, politics, and cultural communities.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Give the following about the decolonization of Africa, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, and Angola fought wars of independence against this European country with capital at Lisbon.
parts.answer: Portugal (accept Portugese Republic)

parts.label: B
parts.question: In the late twentieth century, this former British colony lost power over several of its neighboring territories, such as Namibia and Lesotho [leh-soo-too].
parts.answer: South Africa (accept Republic of South Africa or RSA)

parts.label: C
parts.question: This former French colony’s National Liberation Front, or FLN, won its independence in an eight-year war that ended with the Evian Accords.
parts.answer: Algeria (accept People’s Democratic Republic of Algeria)

topics.description: Hatshepsut was an Eighteenth-Dynasty Egyptian pharaoh who ruled as king alongside Thutmose III and commissioned major building projects, including her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Male holders of this position practiced polygamy but privileged a single “Great Royal Wife,” a title bestowed on such people as Twosret (twahs-RET). Crowns called hedjet (HEJ-et) and deshret (DESH-ret) were used by holders of this position. A holder of this position was buried at (*) Saqqara (saa-KAH-rah) in a step pyramid designed by Imhotep (IM-hoh-tep). A female holder of this position wore false beards during the Fifteenth Dynasty and co-ruled with Thutmose III (TUT-mohs the third). Djoser (JOH-ser) and Hatshepsut (hot-SHEP-set) were holders of, for 10 points, what title for monarchs of ancient Egypt?
parts.answer: Egyptian pharaoh [prompt on king of Egypt]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: According to Herodotus, the first female ruler of this civilization was the semi-mythical empress Nitocris, whom Herodotus associated with Menkaure. This civilization was ruled from Amarna by the husband of Nefertiti. Another female ruler of this civilization, Hatshepsut, wore masculine clothing to represent the sun god Ra. For ten points, name this ancient African civilization that ruled the area around the Nile river.
parts.answer: ancient Egyptians (accept Old Kingdom before “Amarna” is read)

topics.description: The 9 CE battle in which Germanic forces led by Arminius destroyed three Roman legions commanded by Publius Quinctilius Varus.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Tacitus (TASS-it-us) wrote an ethnography about this region describing such groups as the Ingaevones  (ing-ai-VOH-nays). For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [10] Name this region to the north of the Roman Empire, also inhabited by the Marcomanni (MAR-kohMAH-nee) and Alemanni (AH-lay-MAH-nee). Romans were killed here during a battle in which Arminius  (ar-MIN-ee-us) betrayed Varus.
parts.answer: Germania [or Germany]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [10] After this 9 AD battle in Germania, at which Roman forces were destroyed by the Cherusci (chayROO-skee), Augustus supposedly said, “Quintilius (kwin-TIL-ee-us) Varus, give me back my legions!”
parts.answer: Battle of the Teutoburg (TOY-toh-burg) Forest [or Teutoburger Wald]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [10] Germania was often defined as being east of this river in present-day western Germany. A “land”  named for this river included Cologne.
parts.answer: Rhine River

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This ruler apocryphally shouted, “Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!” after losing the Battle of Teutoburg Forest. This ruler secured power by winning the 31 B.C. Battle of Actium. This ruler formed the Second Triumvirate with Marcus Lepidus and (*) Mark Antony in order to defeat his uncle’s assassins. For 10 points, name this nephew of Julius Caesar, who became the first Roman Emperor.
parts.answer: Caesar Augustus [or Octavian] <Ancient/Other History–Rao>
